cards.title: Komlós conjecture
cards.formal: Is there a real constant \(C>0\) such that for every pair of integers \(m,n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m A_{ij}^2\le1\) for each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), there exists a single sign vector \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) for which \[\max_{1\le i\le m}\left|\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\right|\le C?\] The constant must be independent of both dimensions and all matrix entries.
cards.definitions: For a real vector \(v=(v_1,\ldots,v_m)\), its Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\), and its maximum-coordinate norm is \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The columns \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) of \(A\) may be any vectors in \(\mathbb R^m\) with \(\|v_j\|_2\le1\), including zero vectors and vectors with negative or irrational entries. The signed sum is \(Ax=\sum_j x_jv_j\), where every one of the \(n\) coefficients is exactly \(-1\) or \(1\). Define the combinatorial discrepancy \(\operatorname{disc}(A)=\min_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\|Ax\|_\infty\); this minimum is attained because there are finitely many sign vectors. The proposition asks for a universal upper bound on this number over all such matrices. The same chosen \(x\) must satisfy every row inequality simultaneously, though it may depend on the full matrix. The column norm bound is individual, not an average across columns; there is no row norm, row-count, rank or sparsity restriction. All matrices are finite, with arbitrary positive dimensions. The task is existence of some finite constant, not determination of the optimal constant and not an algorithm for finding the signs. There is no bit encoding or computational-time restriction on the entries or the sign choice. A fractional vector in \([-1,1]^n\), a vector with unassigned zero coordinates, or independent choices of signs for different rows does not constitute the required witness.

context_blocks.text: Each column represents one choice that can be assigned a plus or minus sign; each row measures the resulting imbalance in one constraint. Euclidean normalization limits the total squared contribution of a single choice across all constraints. The challenge is to control their maximum imbalance with one common assignment. For any fixed matrix the discrepancy is finite; the universal assertion concerns one bound valid for every number of choices and constraints.

If \(B\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) is an incidence matrix with at most \(t\ge1\) ones in each column, then \(A=B/\sqrt t\) has column Euclidean norms at most one. A Komlós bound \(C\) would therefore give \(\operatorname{disc}(B)\le C\sqrt t\), which is the Beck–Fiala conjecture. An incidence matrix encodes membership of each of \(n\) elements in each of \(m\) sets. The general real-matrix formulation contains this normalized special case, but does not impose its sparsity or entry restrictions.

Banaszczyk’s 1998 theorem gives the classical \(O(\sqrt{\log n})\) bound in the number of columns. Bansal, Dadush and Garg’s 2019 Theorem 2 gives an efficient randomized algorithm attaining that order. These are full-signing bounds, but their growth with \(n\) leaves the dimension-independent conjecture open. The present card does not add the algorithmic requirement that those stronger constructive results satisfy.

Bansal and Jiang’s original Theorem 1.2 improves the bound to \(\widetilde O((\log n)^{1/4})\), where the suppressed factors are powers of \(\log\log n\). Their August 2026 exposition states the bound explicitly as \(O((\log n)^{1/4}(\log\log n)^{7/4})\). These asymptotic expressions concern sufficiently large \(n\); constants can absorb the finitely many small dimensions. The exponent is one quarter, not four. The bound refutes Hajela’s proposed growing lower bound of order \(\sqrt{\log n}\), but it neither proves nor disproves Komlós’s constant bound.

Ercan’s preprint of 8 September 2026 states, for every admissible \(m\times n\) matrix, \[\operatorname{disc}(A)\le2395\left(1+\log_+(n/9)\right)^{1/4}+2\sqrt2,\qquad\log_+(u)=\max\{0,\ln u\}\quad(u>0).\] This removes the iterated-logarithm factor in the claimed upper bound but still grows with \(n\). The paper reports Lean formalizations with the Bansal–Jiang covariance theorem as an external research-theorem assumption; neither those files nor the new proof were independently verified here. Its existence theorem has no estimated bit-model running time.

Guo, Fang and Lu’s preprint submitted on 10 September 2026 claims the full constant bound: for every admissible matrix, \(\operatorname{disc}(A)<3\sqrt{2\pi}\). Its Theorem 1.1 covers arbitrary real vectors, all positive dimensions and every column norm at most one. If correct, it proves the exact existence target here, and its Corollary 1.2 gives the corresponding Beck–Fiala bound. The authors explicitly make no polynomial-time construction claim. This review checked agreement of the theorem statement with the card, but did not independently verify the complete new proof; the status is therefore uncertain.

As a concrete optimization connection, the ESA 2026 paper by Gribanov and coauthors derives algorithms for integer linear programs whose parameter dependence is expressed using Komlós discrepancy bounds. Its published abstract states that the conjecture would reduce the relevant dependence on the number of constraints to a single exponential, with the other stated input parameters retained. This is a conditional application of the conjecture, not evidence that it has been proved.

cards.why: Komlós asks whether controlling the Euclidean size of each vector is enough to balance all coordinates by signs with a dimension-independent error. This is a central link between vector geometry and simultaneous rounding of linear constraints. It would imply the Beck–Fiala bound for sparse set systems and strengthen discrepancy-based guarantees in optimization.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the proposition with a specified finite real constant \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\) there exist positive integers \(m,n\) and a real matrix \(A\) with all column Euclidean norms at most one, such that for every \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) there is a row \(i\) satisfying \(|\sum_j A_{ij}x_j|>C\). Equivalently, a negative answer proves that these discrepancies are unbounded; the dimensions and matrix may depend on \(C\), without an efficient construction requirement. A fixed finite lower bound on the necessary constant does not refute the conjecture. A bound that grows with a dimension, a partial coloring, or a result limited to sparse, random or nonnegative matrices does not prove the universal target. No optimization of the positive constant is required.

cards.title: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G=(V,E)\) admit an orientation \(D\) of all its edges and a function \(f:E\to\{1,2,3,4\}\) such that, at every vertex \(v\in V\), \[\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{head}_D(e)=v}f(e)=\sum_{e\in E:\,\operatorname{tail}_D(e)=v}f(e)\] as an equality of integers?
cards.definitions: A finite loopless undirected multigraph has a finite vertex set \(V\) and a finite set \(E\) of distinct edge identities, each assigned an unordered pair of two distinct vertices. Multiple edges with the same pair of endpoints are allowed and counted separately in every sum. Two vertices lie in the same connected component when a finite sequence of incident edges joins them; a vertex is joined to itself by the empty sequence. A bridge is an edge whose deletion, with the vertex set retained, increases the number of connected components. Bridgeless means that no edge has this property. Disconnected graphs, isolated vertices and the graph with no vertices are allowed. An orientation chooses, for each edge, one endpoint as its tail and the other as its head. The orientation and all values are chosen together for the whole graph; conservation must hold at all vertices simultaneously. Empty sums equal zero. For an integer \(k\ge2\), a nowhere-zero \(k\)-flow in this convention has the same conservation law and values in \(\{1,\ldots,k-1\}\). Thus a 5-flow uses four possible positive integer values; it may use any subset of them. Equivalently, after fixing an arbitrary reference orientation, signed integer values \(z(e)\) with \(1\le|z(e)|\le4\) may be used: a negative value is represented by reversing that edge and taking its absolute value. Values are scalar integers, not vectors, and conservation is exact, not merely a congruence. There are no sources, sinks, externally prescribed demands, capacities, embedding, degree restrictions or construction-time requirements. The proposition is universal over finite graphs, with the orientation and values allowed to depend on the graph.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this universal existence proposition, or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph \(G\) such that for every orientation \(D\) and every assignment \(f:E(G)\to\{1,2,3,4\}\), at least one vertex violates the integer conservation equality. A negative answer must prove both the graph hypotheses and the nonexistence of every permitted flow; failure of one orientation, one search method or a finite collection of trial assignments is insufficient unless it establishes that universal nonexistence. A positive answer must cover every size and all allowed parallel edges and components. A 6-flow, an assertion only for graphs with an additional restriction, or a statement conditional on an unproved conjecture does not settle this target. An alternative formulation can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication establishing the exact proposition or its negation. No efficient procedure for constructing the witness is required.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether the necessary absence of bridges always permits bounded nonzero integer circulation, with the universal value limit improved from five to four. It connects flow existence with graph coloring through planar duality and has a quantitative consequence for packing sets of arcs that meet every directed cut.

importance.reason: A defining flow-existence conjecture with consequences for graph decompositions, orientations and directed-cut packing.

references.title: 5-flow conjecture
references.locator: Preserved discovery provenance from the card’s 11 September 2026 review; this pass grounds the formulation and current-status account in the primary papers above, not a fresh inspection of this community page.

progress.text: Seymour’s universal 6-flow theorem and Younger’s algorithmic version give the neighboring upper bound with integer values at most five, as recalled in the inspected 2025 Theorem 5.
The published dijoin-packing paper explicitly states the 5-flow conjecture and quantifies its consequence for disjoint dijoins.
Li and Su’s publisher abstract reports the 5-flow conjecture for bridgeless graphs of Euler genus at most 20; the unrestricted genus case remains outside that result.
New bounds for vector-valued flows coexist with an explicit statement of the ordinary 5-flow conjecture in Conjecture 1.3.
The latest inspected reconfiguration revision refutes connectivity of the space of 5-flows under cycle changes, while still presenting ordinary 5-flow existence as conjectural.

context_blocks.text: Flow conservation models circulation with no accumulation at any vertex. If an edge is a bridge, summing conservation on one side of that bridge would force its value to be zero. Bridgelessness is therefore necessary. The issue is whether it is sufficient with the fixed range \(1,2,3,4\), independently of graph size. Components can be treated separately, and edgeless components satisfy conservation with the empty assignment. This extends the connected formulation in Conjecture 3 without changing the mathematical target.

Seymour’s 1981 6-flow theorem supplies values in \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) for every bridgeless graph. Younger’s 1983 work gives a polynomial-time construction, as recalled in Theorem 5 of the 2025 paper. The missing assertion is the universal reduction of the maximum value from five to four. The construction-time improvement in the known theorem is additional to the existence requirement on this card.

Tutte’s integer/group-flow theorem equates existence of a nowhere-zero integer 5-flow with existence of a flow over \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\), the residues modulo five, using nonzero values and conservation in that group. This equivalence is an existence theorem; simply interpreting the same residues as positive integers need not preserve integer conservation. Theorem 2.3 in the 2026 reconfiguration paper recalls the lifting statement.

For a connected bridgeless graph drawn in the plane without crossings, the dual graph has a vertex for each face and an edge crossing each original edge between its incident faces. Tutte’s duality identifies existence of an integer \(k\)-flow with a proper \(k\)-coloring of that dual: adjacent dual vertices receive different colors. This explains why flow questions extend coloring phenomena beyond graphs with a planar embedding.

A directed cut consists of all arcs crossing a nontrivial vertex partition when every crossing arc points in the same direction; a dijoin is a set of arcs meeting every such cut. Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi’s Theorem 3 implies that, when the underlying graph admits a 5-flow, a digraph with finite minimum directed-cut size \(\tau\ge2\) contains \(\lfloor\tau/5\rfloor\) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins. The established 6-flow theorem yields \(\lfloor\tau/6\rfloor\). The 5-flow conjecture would improve this guarantee without asserting Woodall’s full packing equality.

Li and Su’s 2025 publisher abstract reports a 5-flow for every bridgeless graph of Euler genus at most 20. Euler genus is the least surface parameter admitting a crossing-free drawing: twice the number of handles for an orientable closed surface, or the number of crosscaps for a nonorientable one. This is a restricted graph class; no uniform bound on genus is assumed here. The present review inspected that abstract, not the full proof.

Esperet and coauthors’ July 2026 revision gives a graph with existing nowhere-zero 5-flows that cannot all be connected by steps changing a flow only along a cycle, while keeping every intermediate flow nowhere zero. Their Theorem 3.4 refutes this reconfiguration property in both the integer and modulo-five settings. It does not refute existence of a 5-flow; their introduction retains Tutte’s conjecture and the 6-flow theorem as the general benchmark.

Li, Li, Luo and Su’s January 2026 paper defines flows with vector values in several real dimensions and proves bounds on their norms. Its Conjecture 1.3 separately states the ordinary one-dimensional 5-flow question. A higher-dimensional flow has additional freedom and does not itself supply the scalar integer assignment required here.

A complete Lean proof must establish universal existence or certify a bridgeless counterexample; special graph classes, vector flows and reconfiguration results do not settle that question.

cards.context:
Flow conservation models circulation with no accumulation at any vertex. If an edge is a bridge, summing conservation on one side of that bridge would force its value to be zero. Bridgelessness is therefore necessary. The issue is whether it is sufficient with the fixed range \(1,2,3,4\), independently of graph size. Components can be treated separately, and edgeless components satisfy conservation with the empty assignment. This extends the connected formulation in Conjecture 3 without changing the mathematical target.

Seymour’s 1981 6-flow theorem supplies values in \(\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) for every bridgeless graph. Younger’s 1983 work gives a polynomial-time construction, as recalled in Theorem 5 of the 2025 paper. The missing assertion is the universal reduction of the maximum value from five to four. The construction-time improvement in the known theorem is additional to the existence requirement on this card.

Tutte’s integer/group-flow theorem equates existence of a nowhere-zero integer 5-flow with existence of a flow over \(\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z\), the residues modulo five, using nonzero values and conservation in that group. This equivalence is an existence theorem; simply interpreting the same residues as positive integers need not preserve integer conservation. Theorem 2.3 in the 2026 reconfiguration paper recalls the lifting statement.

For a connected bridgeless graph drawn in the plane without crossings, the dual graph has a vertex for each face and an edge crossing each original edge between its incident faces. Tutte’s duality identifies existence of an integer \(k\)-flow with a proper \(k\)-coloring of that dual: adjacent dual vertices receive different colors. This explains why flow questions extend coloring phenomena beyond graphs with a planar embedding.

A directed cut consists of all arcs crossing a nontrivial vertex partition when every crossing arc points in the same direction; a dijoin is a set of arcs meeting every such cut. Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi’s Theorem 3 implies that, when the underlying graph admits a 5-flow, a digraph with finite minimum directed-cut size \(\tau\ge2\) contains \(\lfloor\tau/5\rfloor\) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins. The established 6-flow theorem yields \(\lfloor\tau/6\rfloor\). The 5-flow conjecture would improve this guarantee without asserting Woodall’s full packing equality.

Li and Su’s 2025 publisher abstract reports a 5-flow for every bridgeless graph of Euler genus at most 20. Euler genus is the least surface parameter admitting a crossing-free drawing: twice the number of handles for an orientable closed surface, or the number of crosscaps for a nonorientable one. This is a restricted graph class; no uniform bound on genus is assumed here. The present review inspected that abstract, not the full proof.

Esperet and coauthors’ July 2026 revision gives a graph with existing nowhere-zero 5-flows that cannot all be connected by steps changing a flow only along a cycle, while keeping every intermediate flow nowhere zero. Their Theorem 3.4 refutes this reconfiguration property in both the integer and modulo-five settings. It does not refute existence of a 5-flow; their introduction retains Tutte’s conjecture and the 6-flow theorem as the general benchmark.

Li, Li, Luo and Su’s January 2026 paper defines flows with vector values in several real dimensions and proves bounds on their norms. Its Conjecture 1.3 separately states the ordinary one-dimensional 5-flow question. A higher-dimensional flow has additional freedom and does not itself supply the scalar integer assignment required here.

cards.title: Permanent versus determinant
cards.formal: Over \(\mathbb C\), is the determinantal complexity of the permanent not bounded above by any polynomial? Precisely, writing \(d_n=\operatorname{dc}_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)\) as defined below, is it true that for every triple of integers \(B,k,N\ge1\) there is an integer \(n\ge N\) with \(d_n>B(n+1)^k\)? The matrices in the definition are unrestricted exact affine-linear representations over \(\mathbb C\).
cards.definitions: For an integer \(n\ge1\), let \(X=(x_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}\) consist of \(n^2\) algebraically independent commuting variables over \(\mathbb C\). Let \(S_n\) be the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and set \(\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}\). For any \(m\times m\) matrix \(M\) over a commutative ring, \(\det(M)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{a=1}^m M_{a,\pi(a)}\), where \(\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{|\{(a,b):a<b,\ \pi(a)>\pi(b)\}|}\). Define \(d_n\) to be the least integer \(m\ge1\) for which there exist constant matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}\), one \(A_{ij}\) for each input variable, such that \[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\det\!\left(A_0+\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n x_{ij}A_{ij}\right)\] as an identity in \(\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]\). Thus every entry is a constant plus an arbitrary complex linear combination of all input variables. Equality means equality of every coefficient, equivalently equality for every complex assignment, not just Boolean assignments. Finite representations exist, so the minimum is defined; for example the known bound \(d_n\le2^n-1\) suffices. The resource is the matrix dimension \(m\), not its number of entries, coefficient bit lengths or time to find the matrices. Constants can be arbitrary complex numbers, independently for each \(n\), with no computability or uniform construction requirement. Variables may be reused in any number of entries. No symmetry, sparsity, rank condition on \(A_0\), sign restriction, read-once property or restriction on cancellation is imposed. A limit of determinants is not an exact representation unless some permitted matrix already has determinant equal to the permanent. Since every \(d_n\) is finite, the formal assertion is equivalent to nonexistence of integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfying \(d_n\le B(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\ge1\): finitely many exceptions to an upper bound can be absorbed into \(B\). The stated lower-bound quantifiers require arbitrarily large violating indices for every proposed polynomial, not eventual domination of that polynomial at every sufficiently large index.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the quantified lower-bound proposition, or of its logical negation: there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that for every \(n\ge1\) there exist an integer \(1\le m\le B(n+1)^k\) and complex matrices \(A_0,A_{ij}\) satisfying the exact polynomial identity above. A negative answer may prove existence of this nonuniform family without an algorithm to generate its constants. A positive answer must exclude all allowed affine-linear matrices for the relevant \(n,m\), including those that break the permanent’s symmetries. A fixed-degree polynomial lower bound, a bound restricted to real coefficients or a restricted matrix class, or a lower bound for a different polynomial does not prove the proposition. A polynomial-size limiting representation alone does not refute this exact target.
cards.why: The permanent and determinant have almost identical permutation formulas, but the determinant is a basic efficiently computable polynomial whereas the permanent encodes algebraic counting. This conjecture asks whether enlarging the matrix and changing all its entries to affine forms can bridge that difference at polynomial cost. A superpolynomial lower bound would exclude an entire central model of algebraic computation, including polynomial-size algebraic branching programs and formulas.

context_blocks.text: The determinant attaches a permutation sign to each product that the permanent sums without signs. Simply changing signs on the original \(n\times n\) matrix is a very special representation; this card permits arbitrarily larger matrices and arbitrary affine entries. Its size parameter is \(n\), while the number of independent input variables is \(n^2\). Polynomial boundedness in either parameter is equivalent, but the distinction matters when describing a quadratic lower bound.

An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a source and sink, whose edges carry affine-linear forms; it computes the sum, over source-to-sink paths, of the products of their edge labels. Polynomial-size branching programs and polynomial-size determinantal representations simulate each other with polynomial overhead. General arithmetic circuits are directed acyclic computations using addition and multiplication and may reuse earlier results more freely. The algebraic class \(\mathrm{VP}\) permits polynomial-size circuits for families with polynomially bounded degree and number of variables; \(\mathrm{VNP}\) additionally permits summation over polynomially many Boolean variables. The permanent is complete for \(\mathrm{VNP}\). A polynomial-size determinant family for it would imply \(\mathrm{VP}=\mathrm{VNP}\), but the requested superpolynomial determinant lower bound by itself is not a separation from every unrestricted arithmetic circuit.

Mignon and Ressayre’s characteristic-zero theorem gives \(d_n\ge n^2/2\), while Grenet’s construction gives \(d_n\le2^n-1\). The quadratic lower bound is only linear in the permanent’s \(n^2\) variables and falls short of excluding every polynomial. The 2026 Bogart–Valero introduction still presents a quadratic-versus-exponential gap for the ordinary permanent; its new bounds concern generalized permanent families. Historical or recent bounds for another polynomial are not automatically permanent bounds.

Landsberg and Ressayre’s Theorem 2.8 proves the \(2^n-1\) lower bound for \(n\ge3\) when a representation respects the action of left multiplication by permutation and invertible diagonal matrices, and Grenet’s construction meets it. This theorem restricts how symmetries of the input polynomial lift to the representation. It imposes more than the exact identity defining \(d_n\). No symmetry requirement of this kind is part of the question.

Orzel and coauthors define a Boolean sum by first identifying all selected variable positions with one new variable \(y\), then adding the results for \(y=0\) and \(y=1\). This is a two-term sum, even when two positions are selected. Their Theorem 6 proves that for at most two selected positions the permanent can absorb this operation through a simple projection with dimension increased by at most three, while no fixed additive dimension increase works uniformly for the determinant. A simple projection substitutes constants or individual variables and uses each surviving variable at most once, allowing a nonzero overall scalar. This restricted, constant-additive-cost distinction leaves the unrestricted polynomial-size affine representations in this card open.

Border determinantal complexity also admits coefficientwise limits of fixed-dimension determinant representations; their matrix coefficients may vary and become unbounded along the limit. It is at most exact determinantal complexity. Thus a border lower bound implies the same exact lower bound, while an exact lower bound does not automatically exclude limiting representations. Changing the coefficient field also changes the model: allowing \(\mathbb C\) can reduce complexity compared with \(\mathbb R\), and in characteristic two the permanent equals the determinant. These variants cannot silently replace the fixed complex-field target.

Sheshadri’s June 2026 preprint claims a quadratic border lower bound for the diagonal power sum \(\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^n\). That polynomial has \(n\) variables and is not the \(n\times n\) permanent. The inspected theorem therefore does not close this card’s gap, regardless of its stronger dependence on the number of variables. The preprint proof has not been independently verified here.

cards.title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), and integers \(C,c\ge1\), such that \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps on every binary input of length \(L\) and every sequence of its random bits, and has the following correctness property? For every prime \(p\), every generator \(g\) of the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), and every \(h\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), given the binary encoding of \((p,g,h)\) specified below, it outputs the unique integer \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-2\}\) satisfying \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\) with probability at least \(2/3\).
cards.definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_p\) consists of residues \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo the prime \(p\). Its multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\) is \(\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) with multiplication modulo \(p\). The promise that \(g\) is a generator means that \(g^0,g^1,\ldots,g^{p-2}\), reduced modulo \(p\), list these \(p-1\) residues without repetition; hence the requested exponent exists and is unique. Each input integer is represented by its ordinary base-two expansion \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\), without leading zeros and with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Writing \(\ell(a)=|\operatorname{bin}(a)|\), set \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^{\ell(a)}0\operatorname{bin}(a)\). The complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(p)\operatorname{code}(g)\operatorname{code}(h)\), with \(p\) prime and \(1\le g,h<p\). Its length \(L=2(\ell(p)+\ell(g)+\ell(h))+3\) is \(\Theta(\log_2 p)\) on promised inputs. A successful output is exactly \(\operatorname{bin}(x)\); any different output or a designated failure symbol is unsuccessful. For \(p=2\), the sole promised pair is \(g=h=1\) and the answer is \(x=0\). The machine has a fixed finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes and an output tape; each transition costs one step, and any random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. The time bound includes input processing, bit arithmetic, random-bit generation, output and all preprocessing. The same \(A,C,c\) work for every input, with no advice, oracle, precomputed table or supplied factorization of \(p-1\). Arbitrary classical computations on the concrete binary residues are permitted, not just generic group operations. Malformed encodings may be rejected as failure; on well-formed triples outside the mathematical promise, only the global time bound is required. The success guarantee is separately for each promised triple, over the machine’s coins, not over a distribution of primes or targets. The question concerns the multiplicative group of a prime field; additive groups, extension fields and elliptic-curve groups are different models.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of \(A,C,c\) with both the all-input, all-random-sequence time bound and the per-promised-input success guarantee, or a Lean-checked proof that no such triple exists. Equivalently, a negative answer must prove that every machine obeying some global polynomial clock has a promised input on which its probability of outputting the required exponent is less than \(2/3\). Failure of a particular algorithm, an average-case conjecture for a selected prime distribution, or a lower bound restricted to generic group operations does not establish this negation. A quantum algorithm, success only for selected prime families, or a bound polynomial in \(p\) rather than its bit length does not meet the positive target.
cards.why: Discrete logarithms expose a basic gap between efficient modular exponentiation and our ability to invert it. A uniform classical polynomial-time solver would defeat the corresponding finite-field discrete-logarithm assumptions and solve computational Diffie–Hellman in this setting. An unrestricted impossibility proof would establish a fundamental classical lower bound for a concrete arithmetic problem already solvable in quantum polynomial time.

context_blocks.text: For a supplied \(g\) and exponent \(x\), modular exponentiation takes time polynomial in their bit lengths. Inverting this operation would reveal the shared value \(g^{ab}\) from \(g,g^a,g^b\) in the corresponding Diffie–Hellman setting. This implication does not identify discrete-logarithm hardness with every Diffie–Hellman or encryption-security assumption. The card asks a worst-case algorithmic question; a negative answer alone does not prove average-case hardness for a cryptographic parameter distribution.

Candidate answers are efficiently verifiable by checking \(0\le x\le p-2\) and \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\). Thus, as an elementary consequence of verification, existence of the stated bounded-error algorithm is equivalent to existence of a Las Vegas solver that is never wrong and has a uniform polynomial expected running-time bound on every promised input. Independent verified repetition has bounded expected cost in one direction; truncation at three times an expected-time bound gives success at least \(2/3\) by Markov’s inequality in the other. This does not require every run of a Las Vegas solver to terminate, only probability-one termination and finite expected cost.

Schirokauer’s survey gives a conjectured expected-time NFS bound of the form \(\exp(O((\ln p)^{1/3}(\ln\ln p)^{2/3}))\) in the prime-field regime. This is a heuristic complexity analysis, not an unconditional polynomial-time theorem or an unrestricted lower bound. The displayed scale grows faster than every fixed power of \(\log p\). The 2024 Discrete Logarithm Factory paper separately studies costs shared across fields and targets; any such preprocessing must still fit this card’s complete single-input budget.

Shoup’s lower bound concerns randomly encoded group elements. If \(q\) is the largest prime divisor of a cyclic group’s order, constant success requires \(\Omega(\sqrt q)\) generic group operations in that model. His parameter \(q\) is not the field characteristic \(p\); for this card the group order is \(p-1\). The theorem averages over the random encoding, exponent and algorithm coins. It does not exclude algorithms that use the actual integer residues and their arithmetic structure.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s Theorem 1.1 gives expected time \((p d)^{2\log_2 d+O(1)}\) for the multiplicative group of \(\mathbb F_{p^d}\). For fixed \(p\) and growing extension degree \(d\), this is quasipolynomial in the input size. Substituting \(d=1\) supplies at most a polynomial-in-\(p\) guarantee, not the requested polynomial in \(\log p\). The occurrence of the product \(p d\) in their bound must not be confused with the field order \(p^d\).

Lido’s paper, published in March 2026, also proves a quasipolynomial expected-time theorem in small characteristic. In the inspected version its hypothesis is explicitly \(d>p\) for a field of size \(p^d\), excluding the growing prime-field family with \(d=1\). The source’s field-regime restriction remains part of the theorem even though all these problems share the name discrete logarithm.

Shor’s polynomial-time algorithm uses quantum computation. Wu and coauthors’ August 2026 preprint uses the same prime-field generator-input problem as an explicit classical-hardness assumption for a claim about estimating outputs of adaptive shallow quantum circuits. That assumption is not a proved classical lower bound; the reduction and its quantum resource claims were not independently verified in this review.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
